title: Sumedha refuses
hook: a princess refuses marriage to a king, cuts her hair and argues her way to the order (Therigatha, Sumedha)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isidasi told Bodhi all of it. Your line was the whole story. Did you ask one more question before deciding what you thought? Today, a princess who says no to a king. Day seven hundred ninety-five.

A sword, used for a haircut. Sumedha is a king's daughter in the city of Mantavati, and she has been promised in marriage to another king, Anikaratta. She has heard the nuns teach, and she wants to go forth. Her parents want the wedding. The poem that tells her story is long, and much of it is talk: argument after argument from a young woman who will not be talked out of what she has chosen. Today, how she wins.
screen: `A PRINCESS, PROMISED TO A KING.` → `SHE WANTS TO GO FORTH.` → `ARGUMENT AFTER ARGUMENT.`

segments.voice: First, the argument at home. Sumedha tells her parents she wants to go forth, and they weep and plead: a royal marriage is waiting for her. She answers them with the teaching. Life is short, she says, and pleasures don't last. She reaches for pictures the Buddha's discourses use for sense pleasures: a dream that ends on waking, goods that are only borrowed. She isn't sulking. She's making a case. Second, the hair. When the pleading doesn't stop, she acts. She cuts off her own hair with a sword, shuts the palace doors, and sits down. The poem says she entered the first stage of meditative absorption, right there. Third, the king. Anikaratta arrives, dressed for a wedding, with gold and jewels, and he offers her wealth and every pleasure a kingdom has. She doesn't run, and she doesn't give in. She answers him, as patiently as she argued with her parents. Fourth, the result. In the poem, the king ends up asking her father to let her go forth. She wins, not by slipping away in the night, but by making her case to every person standing in the doorway, until there is no one left to persuade. Her refusal is a no to the wedding, and a yes to something she can explain. That's the shape the poem gives her. She argued her way in.
screen: `SHE ANSWERS HER PARENTS.` · `HAIR CUT, DOORS SHUT, SHE SITS.` · `THE KING ARRIVES WITH GOLD.` · `EVEN THE KING ASKS FOR HER.` · then, large: `SHE ARGUED HER WAY IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand by one decision. Bring to mind a choice you've made that someone questions, or that you keep reopening yourself. Settle. Then say your reasons to yourself, plainly, one by one, the way Sumedha laid hers out. Notice which reasons hold when you say them. If the decision still stands, let yourself stand with it, calmly, for these breaths. If it doesn't, that's worth knowing too. The bell holds the time.
Sumedha refuses. A princess promised to a king, who cut her hair, shut the doors, and argued until even the king asked that she be let go. Today's word.
Your line: she argued her way in. Today, when a choice of yours is questioned, give one clear reason, kindly, instead of giving in or walking out. Day seven hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: In Buddhist traditions, going forth as a nun or monk is a decision families take seriously, and the Therigatha's stories of women who argued for it, like Sumedha's, are read as examples of resolve.

original.note: Pali pabbajja: going forth, leaving home for the monastic life. Sumedha argues her way to it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a princess who ran from her wedding.
what it means: Sumedha refuses a royal marriage, cuts her hair, and argues her parents and the king into letting her go forth.

what a scholar hears: much of the poem is argument, and the pictures she uses for sense pleasures, a dream, borrowed goods, also appear in the Buddha's discourses, as in the Majjhima's Potaliya Sutta.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 54 (Potaliya Sutta: similes for sense pleasures)

notes: All texts are paraphrased; no translation quoted.

Confirm the paraphrase of Thig 16.1: Sumedha, daughter of King Konca of Mantavati, betrothed to King Anikaratta (of Varanavati); her parents' pleading; her arguments on impermanence and sense pleasures; cutting her hair with a sword, shutting the palace doors and entering the first jhana; Anikaratta arriving adorned with gold and jewels; and that the king himself asks her father to let her go forth.
The similes 'a dream' and 'borrowed goods' for sense pleasures: confirm that Sumedha uses them (they are standard in MN 22 and MN 54). Cut either if not in her verses.
The past-life section at the end of the poem (her gift in the time of the Buddha Konagamana) is left out.
Editor pass: hook closing line varied from the 'Today's lesson is' formula; sword: some translations read knife; confirm.
Audit: cut 'while the household waited outside' and 'she comes out' (staging not in the poem as paraphrased); the script now says only that she answers the king. Fork setup and reveal matched.
